title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification (MRP)
text:
Theory in brief



Let c index poststratification cells within area j and time t. The cells are defined by whichever population variables are available for poststratification. In a unit-level MRP approach, a binary walking outcome can be modelled at the respondent level as

\begin{aligned}
Y_{ijt} &\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ijt}) \\
\mathrm{logit}(\pi_{ijt}) &=
\alpha + z_{ijt}^{T}\beta + u_j + v_t .
\end{aligned}

where z_{ijt} is a vector of respondent-level predictors used to define or adjust the poststratification cells, \beta contains their coefficients, u_j is an area effect, and v_t is a time effect. The fitted model gives predicted cell means for the binary frequent-walking indicator in each poststratification cell:

\hat{\pi}_{jtc}
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(Y \mid j,t,c).

The poststratification step combines those cell predictions with population counts N_{jtc} available or estimated for the same cells. Area-time estimates are then population-weighted averages of the cell predictions. 
\hat{\mu}_{jt}^{\mathrm{MRP}}
=
\frac{\sum_c N_{jtc}\hat{\pi}_{jtc}}
{\sum_c N_{jtc}}.

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification (MRP)
text:
Estimation approach






Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of Adults who walk for transport daily
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025




MRP extends the unit-level SAE workflow by combining a respondent-level outcome model with a poststratification table describing the target population. For our estimand, we model the binary frequent-walking indicator using age_band (to reflect the age composition in the poststratification table), sex, car_access, and spatial and temporal random effects. We then produce predicted cell means for the binary frequent-walking indicator for each age_band × sex × car_access population cell and aggregate them to MSOA-year estimates using population weights. Uncertainty is propagated by repeating this aggregation across posterior draws.
One data limitation is that the available ONS poststratification table only contains age_band × sex population counts. To include car_access, we first estimate car-access probabilities for each age_band × sex cell and use them to extend the poststratification table. This avoids applying the same MSOA-level car-access share to every age-sex cell, but it introduces additional uncertainty because part of the population table is modelled rather than directly observed. A more conservative alternative would be to model walking using only age_band and sex, and use MSOA-level car-access share separately as a contextual area-level predictor.

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification (MRP)
text:
1 Prepare modelling and poststratification data
As in previous methods, we first create consistent numeric indices for each MSOA and survey year, and a Queen-contiguity adjacency graph for the spatial effect.

area_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["area_id"]]))
time_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["time_id"]]))

area_index <- tibble(
  area_id = area_levels,
  area_inla_id = seq_along(area_levels)
)

time_index <- tibble(
  time_id = time_levels,
  time_inla_id = seq_along(time_levels)
)


msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  inner_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  arrange(area_inla_id)

msoa_neighbours <- poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$area_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)

The MRP workflow needs two inputs:

poststrat_data, the population cells over which predictions are averaged.
model_data, the sampled respondent records used to fit the model;


1.1 Population poststratification data
First, we load the age-sex poststratification table and align its age_band and sex categories with the survey model data.

1.3 Adding car access into poststratification table
The poststratification table has age-sex population counts, but it does not contain the joint distribution of age, sex, and car access. We first model respondent car access using the variables that are available in the poststratification table. We then predict the probability of car_access = 1 for each age-sex-area-time population cell and use those probabilities to expand the poststratification table.


Code
car_access_extension_data <- bind_rows(
  model_data |>
    transmute(
      row_type = "model",
      car_access,
      age_band,
      sex,
      time_inla_id,
      area_inla_id
    ),
  poststrat_age_sex |>
    transmute(
      row_type = "poststrat",
      car_access = NA_real_,
      age_band,
      sex,
      time_inla_id,
      area_inla_id
    )
)

  age_band +
  sex +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE

car_access_extension_fit <- inla(
  formula = car_access_extension_formula,
  data = car_access_extension_data,
  family = "binomial",
  Ntrials = 1,
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1)

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification (MRP)
text:
2 Fit and evaluate models
We fit a sequence of binomial unit-level models. The outcome is the respondent walking indicator, and fitted values for the poststratification rows are returned as response-scale cell means.



Model
Name
Specification




M0
Baseline
Temporal RW1 plus BYM2 spatial MSOA effect


M1
+Demographic
M0 plus age band and sex


M2
+CarAccess
M1 plus respondent car access




m0_formula <- indicator ~
  1 +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m1_formula <- indicator ~
  age_band +
  sex +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m2_formula <- indicator ~
  age_band +
  sex +
  car_access +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

model_formulas <- list(
  "M0 Baseline" = m0_formula,
  "M1 +Demographic" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +CarAccess" = m2_formula
)

The observed respondent rows and the poststratification rows are combined before fitting. Rows with indicator = NA are not used in the likelihood, but INLA still returns their fitted values, which are needed for poststratification.

model_poststrat_data <- bind_rows(
  model_data |>
    transmute(
      row_type = "model",
      indicator,
      age_band,
      sex,
      car_access,
      time_inla_id,
      area_inla_id
    ),
  poststrat_data |>
    transmute(
      row_type = "poststrat",
      indicator = NA_real_,
      age_band,
      sex,
      car_access,
      time_inla_id,
      area_inla_id
    )
)

fit_mrp_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "binomial",
    Ntrials = 1,
    data = model_poststrat_data,
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
  )
}

mrp_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_mrp_model)

As before, we use WAIC as an initial model check. M2 demonstrates the lowest WAIC, meaning the age, sex and car access predictors together best explain the variablity among the binary outcome being modelled.

At this point, having selected our final model, we use poststratification to convert its cell-level predictions into the target MSOA-year estimates. That means, each age_band x sex x car_access cell prediction is weighted by its population count, then aggregated within each MSOA-year. One the one hand, we can apply this calculation using the posterior mean cell values returned above, which gives a simple point-estimate for each cell:

  transmute(cell_mean = mean)

  group_by(area_id, time_id) |>

    weighted_cell_sum = sum(cell_mean * pop_count),
    population_total = sum(pop_count),
    .groups = "drop"

  mutate(mrp_point_estimate = weighted_cell_sum / population_total) |>
  select(area_id, time_id, mrp_point_estimate)

However, the final output for SAE also needs uncertainty estimates. To propagate uncertainty through poststratification, we repeat the same population-weighted aggregation across posterior draws. The posterior draws used for this calculation are shown below.

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification (MRP)
text:
3 Final estimates and uncertainty
The function inla.posterior.sample() gives plausible versions of the fitted model; for each draw, we keep the poststratification rows and convert their fitted values from the logit scale to the original scale of the outcome (0-1).

# Draw plausible versions of the fitted model from the posterior.
set.seed(100)
posterior_draws <- inla.posterior.sample(n = 300, result = mrp_final_fit)

# Rows are poststrat cells; columns are posterior draws; values are predicted cell means.
estimate_draws <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = nrow(poststrat_data), ncol = length(posterior_draws))

predictor_row_index <- startsWith(rownames(posterior_draws[[1]]$latent), "Predictor")

for (draw_id in seq_along(posterior_draws)) {
  draw <- posterior_draws[[draw_id]]
  row_prediction_logits <- as.numeric(draw$latent[predictor_row_index, 1])
  poststrat_logits <- row_prediction_logits[poststrat_cell_rows]
  poststrat_cell_means <- 1 / (1 + exp(-poststrat_logits))
  estimate_draws[, draw_id] <- poststrat_cell_means
}

The matrix estimate_draws contains the draw-level predicted cell means. Using it, we poststratify each posterior draw. That means, for every draw, the predictions are weighted by the corresponding population counts, summed within each MSOA-year, and divided by the total MSOA-year population. This gives one population-weighted estimate per MSOA-year for each posterior draw.

area_year_id <- paste(poststrat_data$area_id, poststrat_data$time_id, sep = "__")

# Population-weight cell means and aggregate them to MSOA-year estimates.
area_year_weighted_sums <- rowsum(estimate_draws * poststrat_data$pop_count, group = area_year_id, reorder = FALSE)
area_year_populations <- rowsum(poststrat_data$pop_count, group = area_year_id, reorder = FALSE)

area_year_means <- area_year_weighted_sums / as.numeric(area_year_populations)

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification (MRP)
text:
Theory in brief



Let c index poststratification cells within area j and time t. The cells are defined by whichever population variables are available for poststratification. In a unit-level MRP approach, a binary walking outcome can be modelled at the respondent level as

\begin{aligned}
Y_{ijt} &\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ijt}) \\
\mathrm{logit}(\pi_{ijt}) &=
\alpha + z_{ijt}^{T}\beta + q_{jt}^{T}\eta + u_j + v_t .
\end{aligned}

where z_{ijt} contains predictors used to define or adjust the poststratification cells, q_{jt} is contextual predictors that do no vary by individual, \beta and \eta contain their coefficients, u_j is an area effect, and v_t is a time effect. The fitted model gives predicted cell means for the binary frequent-walking indicator in each poststratification cell:

\hat{\pi}_{jtc}
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(Y \mid j,t,c,q_{jt}).

The poststratification step combines those cell predictions with population counts N_{jtc} available or estimated for the same cells. Area-time estimates are then population-weighted averages of the cell predictions. 
\hat{\mu}_{jt}^{\mathrm{MRP}}
=
\frac{\sum_c N_{jtc}\hat{\pi}_{jtc}}
{\sum_c N_{jtc}}.

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification (MRP)
text:
Estimation approach






Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of Adults who walk for transport daily
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025




MRP extends the unit-level SAE workflow by combining a respondent-level outcome model with a poststratification table describing the target population. For our estimand, we model the binary frequent-walking indicator using age_band and sex, plus spatial and temporal random effects. We then poststratify, i.e., we produce predicted cell means for each age_band × sex population cell and aggregate them to MSOA-year estimates using population weights provided in the postratification tables. Uncertainty is propagated by repeating this aggregation across posterior draws.
In the modelling step, we can also add contextual predictors, such as MSOA population density, to explain between-area differences. These contextual predictors are area-level variables, so they do not vary between individuals within the same MSOA.
In the poststratification step, our poststratification tables with population counts for each age_band-sex cell for each MSOA were sourced from ONS Mid-year Population Estimates for the 3 periods corresponding to the estimand’s time periods. This ensure the poststratification step adjusts the model predictions for subtle population composition changes throughout the years.

  age_band +
  sex +
  popdens_msoa +

  poststrat_data |>

    family = "binomial",
    Ntrials = 1,
    data = model_poststrat_data,
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)

3 Poststratification
At this point, having selected our final model, we use poststratification to convert its cell-level predictions into the target MSOA-year estimates. That means each age_band x sex cell prediction is weighted by its population count, then aggregated within each MSOA-year.
On the one hand, we can apply this calculation using the posterior mean cell values returned above, which gives a simple point-estimate for each cell:

    weighted_cell_sum = sum(cell_mean * pop_count),
    population_total = sum(pop_count),
    .groups = "drop"

  mutate(mrp_point_estimate = weighted_cell_sum / population_total) |>

title: Area-Level SAE Modeling (Fay–Herriot)”
text:
Theory in brief



The Fay–Herriot model treats each direct estimate as a noisy observation of the true area-time quantity:

\hat{\mu}^{w}_{jt} = \mu_{jt} + e_{jt}, \qquad
e_{jt} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \psi_{jt}),

where \psi_{jt} is the sampling variance estimated from the survey design. The latent area-time mean is then modelled using predictors and an area random effect:

\mu_{jt} = \alpha + \mathbf{x}_{jt}^{T}\boldsymbol{\beta} + u_j.

Here u_j borrows strength across areas while the target remains the area-time quantity \mu_{jt}. The area effect can be replaced by a structured spatial effect, and a temporal effect v_t can be added to represent wave-to-wave dependence. The fitted model gives an area-time estimate by combining the direct estimate with the model prediction:

\hat{\mu}_{jt}^{\mathrm{FH}}
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(\mu_{jt} \mid \hat{\mu}^{w}_{jt}, x_{jt}).

Here u_j borrows strength across areas while the target remains the area-time quantity \mu_{jt}. The area effect can be replaced by a structured spatial effect, and a temporal effect v_t can be added to represent wave-to-wave dependence.

text:
Estimation approach






Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of Adults who walk for transport daily
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025




Area-level SAE starts from the direct estimates created in the previous step. The Fay–Herriot model treats each direct estimate for an area-time cell, an MSOA-year cell in this example, as a noisy observation of the underlying frequent-walking rate, using its sampling variance to control how much confidence the model places in that value.
The model then borrows strength across MSOAs and survey years using spatial and temporal random effects, together with scaled MSOA-level predictors from ONS UK Census 2021, including age and sex summaries, population density, car-access household share, working-from-home share, student share, and occupation profile. This stabilises weak or missing direct estimates while retaining survey-design information.

The missing or zero sampling variances of direct estimates need to be handled, because it controls how much weight each direct estimate receives in the FH model.

For area-time cells without a direct estimate or variance, we assign the maximum observed positive sampling variance, signalling high uncertainty. Their estimates will be mostly model predictions.

title: Area-Level SAE Modeling (Fay–Herriot)”
text:
2 Fit and evaluate models
Each model uses the direct estimate as the response. The sampling variance from the direct estimation is passed to INLA as known observation-level uncertainty, so cells with noisy direct estimates receive less weight. We define these model specifications and fit each one to the direct estimates using INLA.








Model
Name
Specifications




M0
Baseline
Intercept plus independent area effect


M1
+Demographic
M0 plus mean age and proportion female


M2
+Core predictors
M1 plus population density and car-access household share


M3
+All predictors
M2 plus economic activities (full-time students, semi-routine/routine occupation, WFH)


M4
+TempSpatial
M3 plus temporal random walk and BYM2 spatial MSOA effect



The choice of spatial and temporal models should reflect assumptions about how residual variation is structured across space and time.







Temporal model
Description




rw1
First-order random walk: smooths neighbouring time periods.


rw2
Second-order random walk: smooths changes in the trend over longer time series.


ar1
Autoregressive effect: assumes correlation decays with time distance, so closer years are more similar than distant years.










Spatial model
Description




besag
Smooths estimates across neighbouring areas, capturing spatially structured residual variation.


bym2
Updated BYM model with a mixing parameter, phi, which indicates how much residual variation is spatially structured.



With only three survey years, rw1 is suitable because it smooths neighbouring waves. Spatially, bym2 is appropriate because it allows the model to borrow strength from neighbouring MSOAs while still capturing unstructured local variability.

m0_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  1 +
  f(area_inla_id, model = "iid")

m1_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  scaled_mean_age_adult +
  scaled_prob_female +
  f(area_inla_id, model = "iid")

m2_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  scaled_mean_age_adult +
  scaled_prob_female +
  scaled_population_density +
  scaled_car_access_hhshare +
  f(area_inla_id, model = "iid")

m3_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  scaled_mean_age_adult +
  scaled_prob_female +
  scaled_population_density +
  scaled_car_access_hhshare +
  scaled_share_work_from_home +
  scaled_share_students +
  scaled_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(area_inla_id, model = "iid")

m4_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  scaled_mean_age_adult +
  scaled_prob_female +
  scaled_population_density +
  scaled_car_access_hhshare +
  scaled_share_work_from_home +
  scaled_share_students +
  scaled_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  ) +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

model_formulas <- list(
  "M0 Baseline" = m0_formula,
  "M1 +Demographic" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Core predictors" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +All predictors" = m3_formula,
  "M4 +TempSpatial" = m4_formula
)

fit_fh_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_data,
    scale = 1 / model_data$adj_variance,
    control.family = list(
      hyper = list(
        prec = list(initial = 0, fixed = TRUE)
      )
    ),
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE)
  )
}

fh_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_fh_model)







Note



When fitting area-level FH models with INLA, these arguments are needed:

control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE) returns fitted values for every row. In an area-level model, these are the final estimates for each area-time row.
scale passes the inverse sampling variance to INLA, so less precise direct estimates get smoothed more.
control.family fixes the Gaussian residual precision because the direct-estimate variances already provide the uncertainty.
control.compute = list(waic = TRUE) requests WAIC for comparing model fit in case of multiple specifications.



To compare the fitted models’ overall performance, we use WAIC or (Widely Applicable Information Criterion) as a first check. It is a global predictive-fit measure returned by INLA; lower values indicate better expected prediction after penalising model complexity.

title: Setting up for the estimation workflow
text:
1 The Survey Microdata
The tutorial uses a synthetic teaching dataset based on the three survey waves of the National Survey for Wales (NSW) in 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025.
The NSW is a repeated cross-sectional survey of people in Wales, with annual survey periods covering topics such as transport, health, education, public services, housing, internet access, climate change, and the Welsh language. The cleaned microdata combine three survey periods into one harmonised survey microdata.
Since the survey responses are originally geo-indexed at the Local Authority level, but the practical tutorial estimates indicators at MSOA level, we use a synthetic MSOA assignment. The cleaned survey file keeps each respondent’s Local Authority and assigns a synthetic MSOA within that Local Authority using deterministic random allocation. As such, estimates produced from these data should not be read as substantive findings about individual MSOAs in Wales.
This design has two purposes:

Higher spatial resolution for tutorial purposes. Possible to demonstrate MSOA-level direct estimation, area-level SAE, spatial modelling, and MRP-style poststratification.
Privacy and disclosure protection. The assigned MSOA is not the respondent’s true MSOA, so we avoid presenting fine-grained respondent locations.







Note



From here on, the survey period labels are simplified to their end year. For example, the 2020-2021 survey wave is labelled as and referred to as the 2021 wave.

title: Setting up for the estimation workflow

2 Data Preparation Pipeline



Preparation pipeline for analysis-ready inputs



2.1 Defining The Estimand
The estimand is the quantity we want to estimate. It should be defined before preparing the survey indicator or choosing a model, because it determines the outcome coding, denominator, target geography, time period, auxiliary predictors, and poststratification requirements.

Estimate what outcome among which population, across which geography and time period.

In spatio-temporal SAE, this estimand is evaluated for every combination of area and time period. Each combination is an area-time cell: one observation we want to estimate. In this worked example, one area-time cell is one MSOA in one survey wave year, or an MSOA-year cell.
In this tutorial, the estimand is:

title: Unit-Level SAE Modelling (Battese–Harter–Fuller)
text:
Theory in brief



The unit-level route models respondent outcomes directly. For the area-time target \mu_{jt}, a simple mixed-model form is:

Y_{ijt} = \alpha + x_{ijt}^{T}\beta + u_j + v_t + \epsilon_{ijt},

where x_{ijt} contains unit-level predictors, u_j is an area effect, and v_t is a time effect. The area effect can be replaced by a structured spatial effect, and a temporal effect v_t can be added to represent wave-to-wave dependence. To estimate the target for an area-time cell, the fitted model is evaluated using the corresponding population-level auxiliary summaries \bar{x}_{jt}:

\hat{\mu}_{jt}^{\mathrm{BHF}}
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(Y \mid j,t,\bar{x}_{jt}).

text:
Estimation approach






Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of Adults who walk for transport daily
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025




Unit-level SAE models respondent records directly instead of modelling pre-aggregated direct estimates. For our estimand, the Battese–Harter–Fuller model estimates the binary frequent-walking indicator from survey records using unit-level age, sex, and car_access predictors, together with spatial and temporal random effects.
The fitted model is then used to predict the target MSOA-year estimates using MSOA-level summaries of age, sex, and car access, obtained from ONS UK Census 2021. This avoids relying directly on unstable area-level direct estimates, but introduces new assumptions about how adequately or inadequately area-level summaries represent the population composition.

1 Prepare model and aggregation data
Before preparing the model inputs, we create consistent numeric indices for each area and survey year so that INLA can attach random effects to the correct area and period, as well as a Queen-contiguity adjacency graph .adj as input, similar to what we did in the previous FH model estimation.

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

nb2INLA(

text:
2 Fit and evaluate models
We fit linear mixed models to respondent-level records, then use them to predict area-time means. Because the response variable is binary, the fitted values are interpreted as predicted probabilities.
We specify three unit-level models to evaluate at the next step:








Model
Name
Specifications




M1
+TempSpatial
Respondent outcome with a temporal random walk and BYM2 spatial MSOA effect


M2
+Demographic
M1 plus respondent age and sex


M3
+CarAccess
M2 plus respondent-level car access




m1_formula <- indicator ~
  1 +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m2_formula <- indicator ~
  age +
  female +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m3_formula <- indicator ~
  age +
  female +
  car_access +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

model_formulas <- list(
  "M1 +TempSpatial" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Demographic" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +CarAccess" = m3_formula
)

Conceptually, the workflow has two steps: fit the respondent-level model, then evaluate it for each area-time. We implement this by binding the observed respondent rows and the area-time aggregation rows into a single input table before fitting. The area-time rows to have their estimates predicted have indicator = NA, signalling to INLA to return fitted values for them.

model_agg_data <- bind_rows(
  model_data |>
    mutate(row_type = "model"),
  aggregation_data |>
    mutate(
      row_type = "aggregation",
      indicator = NA_real_
    )
) |>
  select(
    row_type, 
    indicator, 
    age, 
    female, 
    car_access, 
    time_inla_id, 
    area_inla_id
    )

fit_bhf_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_agg_data,
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
  )
}

bhf_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_bhf_model)







Note



When fitting unit-level BHF models with INLA, these arguments are needed:

control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE) ensures that fitted values are returned for the full input table, so the predictions for the aggregation rows can be extracted after fitting.
control.compute = list(waic = TRUE) requests WAIC for comparing model fit across candidate specifications.



To compare the fitted models’ overall performance, we again use WAIC as a first check, a global predictive-fit measure returned by INLA. Lower values indicate better expected prediction after penalising model complexity. Here, the lower WAIC for M3 shows that adding the car-access predictor improves the model predictive power as expected.

This limitation can be addressed by using a poststratification table that contains population counts for the joint distribution of the relevant predictors. This is the logic of Multilevel Regression with Poststratification (MRP), predict the outcome for each poststratification cell, then aggregate those predictions using the corresponding population counts so the final estimates better reflect the target population composition.

title: Direct Estimation
text:
Theory in brief



For an area-time cell (j,t), the target is the population mean or proportion:

\mu_{jt} = \frac{1}{N_{jt}}\sum_{i=1}^{N_{jt}} y_{ijt}.

If respondent i has inclusion probability \pi_{ijt} and design weight w_{ijt}=1/\pi_{ijt}, the Horvitz–Thompson ratio estimate is:

\hat{\mu}^{w}_{jt} =
\frac{\sum_{i \in S_{jt}} w_{ijt} y_{ijt}}
{\sum_{i \in S_{jt}} w_{ijt}}.

title: A practical guide to Small Area Estimation for Urban Analytics
text:
Small area estimation for Urban Analytics

Urban researchers often want to use survey data at the scale where urban questions are asked: neighbourhoods, census blocks, transport zones, or other local units. This may involve comparing places, monitoring change over time, identifying local inequalities, or linking survey outcomes to area-level conditions. The problem is that most surveys are not designed to support reliable estimates at all geographic levels and time periods. When responses are broken down by area and year, some cells have only a few respondents and others have none.
This tutorial presents a workflow for choosing spatio-temporal Bayesian small-area estimation (SAE) methods for urban analytics. It focuses on method choice and shows how these approaches can be implemented in INLA.



Bayesian inference and INLA

Bayesian inference is used to combine survey evidence, auxiliary predictors, neighbouring-area structure, year-to-year structure, and uncertainty from sparse cells in one estimation framework. One advantage is that uncertainty of a modelled estimate is returned as posterior distributions for each estimate, which faciliates interpretation in policy contexts.
For code implementation, the examples are fitted with R-INLA, the R interface to Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation. INLA provides deterministic approximate Bayesian inference for latent Gaussian models, usually much faster than MCMC for this workflow.



Tutorial structure

The tutorial is selective. It covers the SAE methods most relevant to common Urban Analytics survey and auxiliary datasets, with the choice driven by outcome type, available survey information, auxiliary data, and population structure.


Estimation setup
Start by specifying the estimand: outcome, target population, areas, and time periods. This defines the area-time cells that need estimates and the inputs required for each possible route.
Direct estimation
Compute survey design-based estimates and sampling variances for observed area-time cells. If these estimates are precise enough and have adequate coverage, direct estimation may be sufficient.
Fay–Herriot area-level model
Use this route when direct estimates exist but are too noisy or incomplete, and the available auxiliary data are area-level predictors. The model smooths direct estimates across predictors, neighbouring areas, and time periods.
Battese–Harter–Fuller unit-level model Use this route when survey microdata are available and the outcome can be modelled at respondent or household level. The fitted unit-level relationship is then aggregated to area-time estimates using area-level summaries of the predictors.
Multilevel Regression with Poststratification (MRP)
Use this route when population counts are available for poststratification cells, such as area by age by sex. The model predicts outcomes for each population cell and weights those predictions back to area-time estimates.




Tutorial data

The tutorial uses synthetic datasets based on the National Survey for Wales.
The maps and estimates illustrate the workflow and should not be interpreted as empirical findings for specific places in Wales. The synthetic dataset construction and preprocessing steps are described in the estimation setup step.



About the project

The tutorial is part of the TRACK-UK project by the City Modelling Lab.
TRACK-UK develops spatial and statistical methods for analysing mobility patterns at fine geographic scales and assessing their implications for transport decarbonisation in the UK. The project works with academic, policy, and industry partners to produce evidence for transport and energy policy.

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
Theory in brief



Let c index poststratification cells within area j and time t. The cells are defined by whichever population variables are available for poststratification. In a unit-level MRP approach, a binary walking outcome can be modelled at the respondent level as

\begin{aligned}
Y_{ijt} &\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ijt}) \\
\mathrm{logit}(\pi_{ijt}) &=
\alpha + z_{ijt}^{T}\beta + q_{jt}^{T}\eta + u_j + v_t .
\end{aligned}

where z_{ijt} is a vector of respondent-level predictors used to define or adjust the poststratification cells, q_{jt} is contextual predictors that do no vary by individual, \beta and \eta contain their coefficients, u_j is an area effect, and v_t is a time effect. The fitted model gives predicted cell means for the binary frequent-walking indicator in each poststratification cell:

\hat{\pi}_{jtc}
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(Y \mid j,t,c,q_{jt}).

The poststratification step combines those cell predictions with population counts N_{jtc} available or estimated for the same cells. Area-time estimates are then population-weighted averages of the cell predictions. 
\hat{\mu}_{jt}^{\mathrm{MRP}}
=
\frac{\sum_c N_{jtc}\hat{\pi}_{jtc}}
{\sum_c N_{jtc}}.

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
Estimation approach






Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of Adults who walk for transport daily
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025




MRP extends the unit-level SAE workflow by combining a respondent-level outcome model with a poststratification table describing the target population. For our estimand, we model the binary frequent-walking indicator using age_band, sex, car_access, and spatial and temporal random effects. We then produce predicted cell means for the binary frequent-walking indicator for each age_band × sex × car_access population cell and aggregate them to MSOA-year estimates using population weights. Uncertainty is propagated by repeating this aggregation across posterior draws.
In the modelling step, we can also add contextual predictors, such as MSOA population density, to explain between-area differences. These contextual predictors are area-level variables, so they do not vary between individuals within the same MSOA.
In the poststratification step, our poststratification tables with population counts for each age_band-sex-car_access cell for each MSOA were sourced from ONS UK Census 2021 so it only observes the composition for 2021 only. For the 2023 and 2025 estimands, the model can still estimate different area-time outcomes through the temporal and spatial terms, but the poststratification weights are held fixed, assuming that local demographic and car-access composition does not change across the survey years. In other words, N_{jtc} = N_{jc,2021} for all three waves.

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
1 Prepare modelling and poststratification data
As in previous methods, we first create consistent numeric indices for each MSOA and survey year, and a Queen-contiguity adjacency graph for the spatial effect.

area_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["area_id"]]))
time_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["time_id"]]))

area_index <- tibble(
  area_id = area_levels,
  area_inla_id = seq_along(area_levels)
)

time_index <- tibble(
  time_id = time_levels,
  time_inla_id = seq_along(time_levels)
)


msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  inner_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  arrange(area_inla_id)

msoa_neighbours <- poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$area_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)

The MRP workflow needs two inputs:

poststrat_data, the population cells over which predictions are averaged.
model_data, the sampled respondent records used to fit the model;


1.1 Population poststratification data
First, we load the age-sex-car poststratification table and align its age_band, sex, and car_access categories with the survey model data.

We fit a sequence of binomial unit-level models. The outcome is the respondent walking indicator, and fitted values for the poststratification rows are returned as response-scale cell means.

  1 +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(

    model = "bym2",

m1_formula <- indicator ~
  popdens_msoa +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m2_formula <- indicator ~
  age_band +
  sex +
  popdens_msoa +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m3_formula <- indicator ~
  age_band +
  sex +
  car_access +
  popdens_msoa +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

model_formulas <- list(
  "M0 Baseline" = m0_formula,
  "M1 +PopdensContext" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Demographic" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +CarAccess" = m3_formula
)

The observed respondent rows and the poststratification rows are combined before fitting. Rows with indicator = NA are not used in the likelihood, but INLA still returns their fitted values, which are needed for poststratification.

model_poststrat_data <- bind_rows(
  model_data |>
    mutate(row_type = "model"),
  poststrat_data |>
    mutate(row_type = "poststrat", indicator = NA_real_
    )
) |>
  select(
    row_type, 
    indicator, 
    age_band, 
    sex,
    car_access,
    popdens_msoa, 
    time_inla_id, 
    area_inla_id
    )

fit_mrp_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "binomial",
    Ntrials = 1,
    data = model_poststrat_data,
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
  )
}

mrp_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_mrp_model)

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
3 Poststratification
At this point, having selected our final model, we use poststratification to convert its cell-level predictions into the target MSOA-year estimates. That means, each age_band x sex x car_access cell prediction is weighted by its population count, then aggregated within each MSOA-year. We can apply this calculation using the posterior mean cell values returned above, which gives a simple point estimate for each cell:


Code
mrp_final_fit <- mrp_fits[["M3 +CarAccess"]]
poststrat_cell_rows <- which(model_poststrat_data$row_type == "poststrat")

cell_mean_predictions <- mrp_final_fit$summary.fitted.values |>
  as_tibble() |>
  slice(poststrat_cell_rows) |>
  transmute(cell_mean = mean)

cell_point_estimates <- bind_cols(poststrat_data, cell_mean_predictions)

area_year_point_estimates <- cell_point_estimates |>
  group_by(area_id, time_id) |>
  summarise(
    weighted_cell_sum = sum(cell_mean * pop_count),
    population_total = sum(pop_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(mrp_point_estimate = weighted_cell_sum / population_total) |>
  select(area_id, time_id, mrp_point_estimate)

However, the final output for SAE also needs uncertainty estimates. To propagate uncertainty through poststratification, we repeat the same population-weighted aggregation across posterior draws. The posterior draws used for this calculation are shown below.
The function inla.posterior.sample() gives plausible versions of the fitted model. For each draw, we keep the poststratification rows, convert fitted values from the logit scale to the original 0-1 scale, population-weight them within each MSOA-year, and summarise the resulting posterior distribution.

# Draw 300 posterior draws of the model fit
set.seed(100)
posterior_draws <- inla.posterior.sample(300, mrp_final_fit)

#  For each draw, keep the poststrat rows, convert values to the original scale 
predictor_rows <- startsWith(rownames(posterior_draws[[1]]$latent), "Predictor")
area_year_id <- paste(poststrat_data$area_id, poststrat_data$time_id, sep = "__")
poststrat_draws <- sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  plogis(as.numeric(draw$latent[predictor_rows, 1])[poststrat_cell_rows])
})

# Population-weight them
area_year_weighted_sums <- rowsum(poststrat_draws * poststrat_data$pop_count,
  group = area_year_id, reorder = FALSE)
area_year_populations <- rowsum(poststrat_data$pop_count,
  group = area_year_id, reorder = FALSE)
area_year_means <- area_year_weighted_sums / as.numeric(area_year_populations)

4 Final estimates and uncertainty
As with previous methods, we report the MRP estimates alongside the direct estimates and variance outputs in order to provide a full view of the direct survey evidence that accompanies the modelled estimates.


Code

  file.path(base_path, "freqwalk_estimates_direct.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  select(area_id, time_id, n, direct_estimate, variance)

final_mrp_results <- final_mrp_results |>
  left_join(direct_estimates, by = c("area_id", "time_id")) |>
  mutate(
    direct_ci_width = 2 * qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(pmax(variance, 0))
  ) |>
  select(
    area_id,
    msoa_name,
    time_id,
    n,
    direct_estimate,
    variance,
    direct_ci_width,
    mrp_estimate,
    mrp_variance,
    mrp_lower,
    mrp_upper,
    mrp_ci_width
  )







It is essential to caveat these estiamtes with the fact that we are reusing the same age-sex-car population composition of one year (2021) to estimate for the other two waves (2023, 2025) and letting the modelled time effect capture changes in the outcome. This is only possible if the relative age_band x sex x car_access poststratification weights stay consistent throughout the target periods, an assumption that must be made transparent.
Compared to estimates obtained from other modelling approaches, the MRP estimates are very close to the BHF estimates, with points clustered around the equality line. Agreement with the direct estimates is much weaker as expected, reflecting the instability of sparse MSOA-year survey cells. The Fay–Herriot estimates tend to sit lower than MRP for many cells, suggesting stronger shrinkage toward lower area-year rates.
